Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: 'Shouting in Arabic' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless there is specific trauma detail indicating the stalker used Arabic; with the rest of the profile, this trigger appears overly specific and disconnected from the other stalking-related items.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same Memory node items describing fragmented, intrusive, partially inaccessible trauma memory ('extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'fragments appear suddenly without warning'). While not impossible, this is a direct enough tension within the node to question coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: Fear of losing control of anger and doing something terrible is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile, which centers on fear, mistrust, stranger threat, and life damage after stalking. It points toward a perpetration/harm-to-others concern not otherwise represented in Threat, Triggers, Memory, or strategies, making the formulation less coherent.

vignette: Clara stood at the edge of the staff lounge, watching the police officer pace the hallway. At twenty-eight, she had come to believe that anyone in uniform carried the same quiet authority as the man who had cornered her two years ago. The stalking had unfolded over six months during her first full academic year, and the memory of it arrived in uneven waves. Some moments stood in stark relief: the exact pitch of the footsteps behind her on the wet pavement, the way the air grew heavy when he stopped moving. Other stretches of time were completely blank, as if she had slept through the worst of it. She knew what happened, yet when her partner asked her to describe the nights, the words would slip away, leaving only a hollow certainty behind. Fragments of the event would surface without warning-a coat brushing a brick wall, a sudden rush of horror-and then dissolve before she could name them. Over the following weeks and months, those experiences settled into her daily rhythm. Clara kept her guard up everywhere. In the school parking garage, she avoided the far corners, certain that the silence there was not empty but watchful. When the room grew unusually quiet, she felt something dangerous about to happen. Strangers approaching her at the grocery store or asking for directions in the hallway felt like invasions, and she would offer hurried answers while her heart hammered against her ribs. Heavy breathing, whether from a student with seasonal allergies or a colleague across a desk, made her shoulders tense. She found herself staying after grading papers, finding comfort in the predictable scratch of her pen, yet she would glance up at the classroom windows, tracking the empty corridors as if someone might still be walking behind her. Her relationship weathered the changes, but her partner noticed how she slept on the edge of the mattress, eyes fixed on the door, always assessing the quiet. Her trust in people had fractured. She had come to believe that her life had been destroyed by the trauma. The fear, the anger, and a quiet shame co-existed in her chest, alongside the conviction that she had to be on guard all the time, the erosion of her routine, and the fractured trust in others. The school year progressed, but she lived in a suspended present, where every hallway crossing and every parked car required assessment. It was the accumulation of sleepless nights and the quiet erosion of her routine that finally brought her to the clinic. She no longer looked forward to the weekends, when the silence in her apartment grew so profound she could feel it pressing against her eardrums. She came to therapy hoping to untangle the knot of her experiences without losing the careful boundaries she had built. She was most afraid of the silence returning, of the feeling of being followed becoming a permanent shadow, but she held onto the hope that she could reclaim her classroom, her relationship, and the words she had lost.
